Operator: today, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Q3 2026 Aecon Group Inc. earnings conference call. At this time, all participants are in listen-only mode. After the speaker's presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question during the session, you will need to press star and one on your telephone. You will then hear an automated message advising your hand is raised. To withdraw your question, please press star and one again. Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to your speaker for today, Adam Borgatti, Senior Vice President of Corporate Development and Investor Relations. Please go ahead.
Adam Borgatti: Thank you, Lisa. Good morning, everyone, and thanks for participating in our call today. Joining me are Jean-Louis Servranckx, President and CEO, Jerome Julier, Executive Vice President and CFO, and Alistair MacCallum, Senior Vice President, Finance. Our earnings announcement was released yesterday evening, and we posted a slide presentation on our website, which we'll refer to during this call. Following comments, we'll be happy to take questions from analysts, and we ask that you keep to one question and a follow-up if necessary before getting back into the queue. As noted on slide two of the presentation, listeners are reminded the information we're sharing with you today includes forward-looking statements based on assumptions that are subject to significant risks and uncertainties. Although Aecon believes the expectations reflected in these statements are reasonable, we can give no assurance that these expectations will prove to be correct. Turning to slide three, I'm pleased to share key highlights and accomplishments from the quarter. Aecon delivered record quarterly revenue of CAD 1.9 billion, increasing 26% over the same period last year. 71% of the revenue growth in the quarter was organic. Adjusted EBITDA improved significantly in the quarter to CAD 130 million compared to CAD 93 million last year, an increase of 40%, driven by strong revenue growth and year-over-year margin improvement in the construction segment. Aecon was awarded contracts and joint ventures with an aggregate value of CAD 3 billion for the Pickering Nuclear Generating Station refurbishment execution phase. Our CAD 1.75 billion share of the contracts was added to backlog in the quarter and represents the largest nuclear award in Aecon's history. The award, along with continued investments in fabrication capacity, reinforces Aecon's position as Canada's nuclear builder, supported by an established record of delivering complex nuclear projects across the full nuclear value chain. Backlog at September 30th was CAD 14.6 billion, up 39% over last quarter, representing the highest reported backlog in Aecon's history and underpinned by a diversified mix of long-term projects with appropriate risk balance. Over 80% of Aecon's backlog is tied to non-fixed price or collaborative fixed-price contract models. We're extremely proud to achieve Gold Partnership Accreditation in Indigenous Relations status, becoming the first construction company with nationwide operations to achieve the highest level of certification. Building strong, respectful relationships with Indigenous peoples and communities has long been part of how Aecon operates. This recognition reflects that history and our commitment to meaningful Indigenous partnerships. We also continue to advance our strategic priorities and concessions, including the launch of Maple Fibre, a strategic alliance to finance, design, build, and own next-generation network infrastructure. Aecon reinforces its positive outlook, supported by the expectation for double-digit revenue growth for the full-year 2026, based on our strategic positioning in sectors with attractive demand profiles, growing recurring revenue programs, and a healthy pipeline of project opportunities. With that, I'll hand the call over to Jerome.
Jerome Julier: Thanks, Adam, and good morning, everyone. I'll speak to Aecon's consolidated results, review results by segment, and then address Aecon's financial position. Turning to slide four, revenue for the three months ended September 30, 2026, of CAD 1.9 billion was up CAD 390 million, or 26%, compared to the same period in 2025. Adjusted EBITDA of CAD 130 million increased 40% compared to CAD 93 million last year, while operating profit of CAD 83 million compared to an operating profit of CAD 61 million in the same period last year. The improvement in the period was driven by higher gross profit of CAD 70 million compared to the same period in 2025. Adjusted diluted earnings per share was CAD 0.86 in the quarter, an improvement compared to CAD 0.49 in the third quarter of last year. Financial results in the quarter were impacted by negative gross profit of CAD 9 million from the legacy projects. The final legacy project reached substantial completion in June and commenced operations in July of this year. Aecon and its joint operations partners continue to pursue commercial resolution on the matter. Backlog of CAD 14.6 billion at the end of the third quarter is the highest reported backlog in its history and compares to backlog of CAD 10.8 billion in the same time last year. New contract awards of CAD 6 billion were booked in the quarter, and CAD 10.1 billion was booked over the trailing 12 months. Now, looking at results by segment. Turning to slide five, construction revenue of CAD 1.9 billion in the third quarter was CAD 410 million, or 27% higher than the same period last year. Construction revenue growth in the quarter was 72% organic and was broad-based with higher revenue in all sectors. The largest increase of CAD 184 million was registered in utilities operations, driven by a higher volume of electrical, gas, and telecommunications work, including contributions from acquisitions completed in the first quarter of 2026. Nuclear operations increased CAD 130 million due to a higher volume of core refurbishment, decommissioning, and engineering services work at nuclear generating stations in Ontario and the United States. Revenue in civil operations increased CAD 45 million, primarily from higher works volume on power and rail projects and in foundations work, partially offset by a lower volume of highway, road, and bridge construction activity. In industrial operations, revenue increased CAD 42 million, primarily from a higher volume of field construction work in the United States, with most of the revenue growth attributable to businesses acquired in the third quarter of 2025, as well from an increase in the industrial components of power generation projects. Urban transportation solutions increased CAD 9 million, driven by a higher volume of subway and commuter rail system work, partially offset by a lower volume on LRT projects that achieved substantial completion or became operational in 2025. Turning to slide six, construction segment adjusted EBITDA of CAD 132 million compared to CAD 88 million last year, with an adjusted EBITDA margin of 6.8% compared to 5.8% in 2025. The increase was primarily driven by an improvement in gross profit margin in civil and nuclear operations. More broadly, and as Jean-Louis will further discuss, the improvements reflect the continued shifts towards a lower-risk work mix, stronger execution, and the gradual normalization of earnings as legacy project exposure winds down. Turning now to slide seven, concessions adjusted EBITDA for the quarter was CAD 12 million compared to CAD 15 million in the same period last year, largely due to the deferral of intercompany construction profit related to network assets under development. Turning to slide eight, at September 30, 2026, Aecon held core cash and cash equivalents of CAD 529 million, which is over and above the CAD 537 million of cash representing Aecon's proportionate share of cash held in joint operations. In addition, at September 30, 2026, Aecon had committed revolving credit facilities of CAD 1 billion, of which CAD 342 million was drawn and CAD 4 million was utilized for letters of credit. Combined with our CAD 960 million EDC performance security guarantee facility, Aecon can access total committed credit facilities, working capital, and letter of credit requirements totaling approximately CAD 2 billion. Net debt at September 30, 2026 was CAD 338 million. This includes only our core cash balances and also recognizes the CAD 320 million repayment agreement for the preferred shares of Aecon Utilities as debt. The repayment continues to be anticipated to close in the fourth quarter of 2026. Net debt-to-trailing 12-month adjusted EBITDA was 1x. Aecon generated free cash flow of CAD 645 million in the trailing 12-month period ended September 30, 2026, compared to CAD -41 million in free cash flow in the same period last year. Cash performance was driven by relentless focus on working capital management and contract structure. At this point, I'll turn the call over to Jean-Louis to address our business performance and outlook.
Jean-Louis Servranckx: Thank you, Jerome. Turning to slide nine, Aecon continues to drive broad-based growth across our nuclear, civil, utilities, industrial, and urban transportation sectors. In the third quarter, the construction segment generated record revenue with increases across all sectors. Power and utility services collectively represent 58% of Aecon's CAD 6.4 billion in trailing 12-month construction revenue. Nuclear is a key part of that position and a genuine differentiator for Aecon, Canada's nuclear builder. Our capabilities span engineering, in-reactor construction, nuclear-qualified fabrication and modularization, refurbishment, decommissioning, and new build in North America. We are acquiring additional fabrication capacity in Ontario, which will expand Aecon's nuclear fabrication network to four facilities in Canada and the United States to support some of the largest nuclear refurbishment and new build projects in North America. Our concessions portfolio also continues to grow and diversify, leveraging our unique project development, financing, and integrated construction capabilities. We recently launched Maple Fibre, a majority-controlled strategic alliance with a Tier-1 telecommunication operator to finance, design, build, and own next-generation network infrastructure. Aecon Concessions own the majority interest in the partnership, and Aecon Utilities has commenced construction for Maple Fibre in Ontario. Turning to slide 10, I want to spend a moment on the strength of our current positioning and the visibility we have into future growth. We ended the quarter with record backlog of CAD 14.6 billion. That backlog tells an important story, but it is really only part of the story. On the right-hand side of the slide, we show 10 major projects where Aecon is currently in development or collaborative delivery phases, but where significant future scope is not yet reflected in backlog. In nuclear, for example, our backlog includes the recently announced Pickering Unit 5 refurbishment and full turbine generator replacement award while future opportunity associated with the refurbishment of Unit 6, 7, and 8 is not yet reflected. Similarly, at Darlington, unit 1 of the new nuclear SMR project is under construction, while the future three units represent additional opportunity and the development for work beyond our current backlog. The same dynamic applies across other major projects and programs shown here, including the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility SMR, the hydroelectric Mactaquac Life Extension Project, the port and marine construction project at Roberts Bank Terminal 2 in Vancouver, the defense project for Arctic Over-the-Horizon Radar Stage 1, and the regional rail network GO Expansion Program, where additional programs under development are opportunities to convert to new work over time. The backlog we do report is long-dated. Approximately two-thirds extends beyond the next 12 months, and about 40% or CAD 6 billion beyond 24 months. Taken together, our reported backlog represent only the fully contracted portion of a much broader portfolio of secured and developing work, providing significant visibility into future growth. Turning to slide 11, trailing 12 months recurring revenue was over CAD 1.1 billion at September 30th, 2026, with recurring revenue from utility services increasing to CAD 987 million from CAD 695 million last year, an increase of 42%. Importantly, this recurring revenue is also not reflected in our reported backlog. Our MSA programs have a weighted average contract term of approximately three years and a near 100% renewal rate, providing significant multi-year visibility beyond the backlog we report today. Aecon Utilities is generating nearly CAD 1 billion of recurring revenue today, with continued growth across Canada and the U.S.. It is an integral part of our growth platform, with capabilities spanning power, transit electrification, battery storage, data center electrical infrastructure, airports, and nuclear development. Turning now to slide 12. We have an unwavering focus on risk-adjusted profitability, highlighted by the relationship between our contract mix and our margin performance. At September 30th, approximately 64% of our backlog was comprised of variable price contracts, which covers cost plus or unit price work. Of the remaining 36% classified as fixed price, close to half of this was booked following collaborative and fully integrated development phases. Taken together, approximately 81% of our CAD 14.6 billion backlog is derived from collaborative model or non-fixed price work. On a trailing 12-month revenue basis, approximately 69% of construction revenue was generated from collaborative or non-fixed price contracts. As our backlog converts into revenue over time, we expect the lower risk profile of our backlog to continue to support greater predictability in our result. This evolution in our risk profile is particularly important when looking at margin. This is the right part of slide 12. Construction trailing 12-month adjusted EBITDA margin had increased from 3.7% in the third quarter of 2025 to 5.6% today, while we have maintained a consistent lower risk revenue profile throughout that period. This slide, 12 of our presentation, is extremely important, and we will come back to it probably during the question. As we have said previously, our focus is on stabilizing and gradually improving margins. We have done it and are focused on driving further improvements in risk-adjusted profitability. Our strategic position in key sectors, lower risk contract mix, stronger execution, and the continued wind-down of legacy project exposure provide a stronger foundation for more predictable performance. Turning to slide 13, Aecon expects double-digit revenue growth in 2026. Our expectation for a broad-based revenue increase in 2026 and further revenue growth in 2027 is underpinned by secure backlog exceeding CAD 14 billion, recurring revenue programs, recent acquisitions, the pipeline of project opportunities tied to nuclear and conventional power, critical resource development, mass transit, water, defense, and digital infrastructure. This clearly positions Aecon at the center of many of the infrastructure priorities Canada needs to deliver over the coming years, while our growing U.S. and international presence provides additional diversification and avenues for growth. In the concession segment, there are several opportunities to add to the existing portfolio of Canadian and international concessions in the next 6 to 12 months to support trends in aging infrastructure, mobility, connectivity, energy, and population growth. Aecon's deliberate shift toward a greater weighting of improved risk-adjusted work program, in combination with a strong focus on operational excellence, is anticipated to support the gradual improvement of adjusted EBITDA margins in the construction segment in 2026 and 2027. Our outlook for 2026 continues to be very positive. We are excited about the momentum we have built so far this year and remain focused on fully executing our strategy to drive long-term shareholder value. Turning now to slide 14, I want to congratulate our Indigenous Relations team for achieving Gold Partnership Accreditation in Indigenous Relations status. This achievement reflects the dedication of teams across Aecon and the strength of the relationships we have built with Indigenous communities, businesses, and partners over many years. We are proud of what we have accomplished and invite our partners to join us in advancing sustained action with lasting benefits for generations to come. In closing, I would like to thank our outstanding team at Aecon. In the quarter, over 14,000 team members across all our operating sectors delivered on our potential with an unwavering safety-always mindset and commitment. We will now turn the call over to analysts for questions.
Operator: Thank you. As a reminder, if you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone. You will then hear the automatic message advising your hand is raised. We also ask that you please wait for your name and company to be announced before proceeding with your question. One moment while we compile the Q&A roster. Our first question will be coming from Yuri Lynk of Canaccord Genuity. Please go ahead.
Yuri Lynk: Good morning, guys.
Jean-Louis Servranckx: [inaudible]
Yuri Lynk: Just want to go back to the margin discussion, and if you could maybe go through some of the puts and takes on how the construction segment margin improves from here. Particularly, if you could address the operating leverage, because there has been a notable increase in SG&A. Also, if mix has anything to do with it.
Jean-Louis Servranckx: Okay. I am going to begin on a general basis, and then Jerome will probably address the last point of your question. We at Aecon, we have been patiently and steadily preparing for this moment and the path forward from here. I used to give to my team the image of the way the helicopter pilots are being trained in the army. They have to get the left eye totally focused on the instruments, which is for us executing project per project the best we can, and the right eye pointing 2 mi or 3 mi ahead, which is about our strategy. It is exactly the same thing that we have at our management team level at Aecon. We consider that we have acquired a strategic and unique positioning on the infrastructure market. We have acquired a de-risked project mix, which is very important, and that will give us a much better margin predictability. This page 12, as I announced it a few minutes ago, is extremely important. If you see the four pure economic figures of the quarter, it means CAD 1.9 billion of revenue, CAD 130 million of EBITDA, a backlog of CAD 14.6 billion, and a creation during the last trailing 12-month of CAD 645 million free cash flow. All this is linked together. This page 12 is quite important. This 80%, 81% of non-fixed price contract or collaborative fixed price contract is the global answer to your question, and it is quite important. Jerome, maybe on those two, three additional questions?
Jerome Julier: Yeah.
Jean-Louis Servranckx: You can follow up for sure.
Jerome Julier: On the margin profile, Yuri, in furtherance to what Jean-Louis just mentioned, margins are increasing when you include the legacy projects, obviously, as the losses increasingly move to the rearview mirror. But if you exclude those losses, what we've seen is a stabilization of the construction margin profile, with the overall risk balance of the business improving. I would describe that almost like as the best of both worlds situation. That was the objective across 2026. Your question is focused on 2027, where we continue to see opportunities to enhance the margin profile. That's informed by the work that we have in backlog and the embedded margins that we see there. But I think one thing that's important is not to get ahead of ourselves. Aecon's executing on a very broad and large long-term portfolio of projects with very strong risk balance, and so we view these things as incremental improvements over time. Just to say that the expectation is to do better. We just don't want them to get ahead of themselves. On the operating leverage, I'd make the observation that SG&A growth in the quarter, the quarter residual, was tied to incentive compensation, M&A costs, and ERP program implementation, and then additional SG&A from companies that we've acquired over the last 12 months. On that basis, there's a decent level of control there. Some of this has to do with where you want to book costs, whether you pile them back up into gross profit, where we've obviously seen a large expansion in margin, or whether you maintain them in the SG&A bucket, which is what we do. At the end of the day, overall, we're seeing an increase in the operating profit margin or adjusted EBITDA profit margin, which I think is the indicator that you want to track against. On the mix front, the overall execution mix that we have in front of us is balanced by client type, by region, by contract model, and by sector. That was the case in the last 12 months. That's the case what we see coming in the future in the next 12 months. I wouldn't see mix as being a determinative factor here.
Yuri Lynk: Okay. Last, just clarification question. Did I hear you say there was CAD 9 million of legacy costs in the construction EBITDA this quarter?
Jerome Julier: That's right.
Yuri Lynk: Okay. Thanks, guys. I'll turn it over.
Jerome Julier: Thanks.
Operator: Thank you. One moment for the next question. Our next question is coming from the line of Chris Murray of ATB Cormark Capital Markets.
Chris Murray: Yeah. Thanks, folks. Good morning. Congratulations on probably a record backlog build. Certainly very positive, and as you noted, lots more to come. I know we're talking about a double-digit number, which I think was sort of expressed to me as higher than 11%, less than 98%. But I think that if we think about the level of growth that you're going to see over probably the next, call it decade, can you talk a little bit about your ability to manage that growth, both in terms of your staffing, both at the construction management level and also at the trade level?
Jean-Louis Servranckx: Yes, I think I can handle this. Obviously, we are extremely focused on our capacity to perfectly execute this backlog. We have been investing during the last years a lot on operational excellence, recruiting, training, motivating our workforce at all level, bringing as much loyalty as we can in a rather hot market. We have been extremely cautious about the mix of our different activities between our different sectors. You don't have the same people renovating tracks or building industrial facilities or working in the nuclear or laying part of electrical grids or pipeline. Those are different kind of people, and our balance of activity helps us on this one. It just means that we do not see, so far, a danger in being able to perfectly execute our backlog.
Chris Murray: Okay. That's helpful. The other question is more around nuclear. I guess we're expecting some sort of decision, I would think, towards the end of the year, maybe from Bruce, maybe from OPG. Can you explain or kind of lay out what would be involved, depending on how those decisions go? There's also some debate about technology selection. Can you talk about your exposure to both CANDU and, if they decide to go Westinghouse, how that would change? Can you maybe elaborate a little bit on what you've acquired in the nuclear business in Ontario for additional support?
Jean-Louis Servranckx: First of all, we are not the one making the decision. Obviously. But what is extremely important for us is the position we have been building in nuclear, where I think we are extremely strong. We are going to refurbish the totality of the 14 CANDU units in Ontario. There is not one single general contractor except Aecon. We are in association with AtkinsRéalis, who has a kind of different scope, but not one single general contractor who has entered into a CANDU reactor for years. So, if the decision is for CANDU, obviously we are extremely well-positioned. This being said, we are also part of the team to build this small modular reactor number 1, which is a GE Hitachi 300 MW boiling water technology. We are one of the only North American contractor who have fabricated already for Westinghouse their very important ASME Q modules. We are also in full steam ahead in our development phase of the Cascade Energy project, which is another kind of reactor, X-energy. It means that whatever the decision, because we are technology agnostic and because we have an incredible workforce at all level, this will obviously favor Aecon. When I read, Aecon, Canada nuclear builder, I tend to say, Canada, the nuclear builder is Aecon. Fabrication is important. It's one of the key success factor of the generation to come. It's about modularization. SMR, I used to say, okay, it's small modular reactor, but it should be standardized modular reactor. It means that this is the key of success, and we are getting stronger and stronger. This is why we have been acquiring an additional facility in Ontario. Maybe, Jerome, you can speak a little about it. This is why we are investing a lot in robotics, and this is why we are extremely focused on tracking all our productivity reports day after day, because it is part of the future. Jerome, you want to speak a little about—
Jerome Julier: Yeah
Jean-Louis Servranckx: —the acquisition and fabrication capacity?
Jerome Julier: Yeah. So, in the release, we announced that Aecon agreed to acquire additional fabrication capacity for the nuclear sector in Ontario. I will probably provide a little bit more detail on that. So, it is going to close in the fourth quarter. Expectation is in the rough area of CAD 50 million. We look to own assets that we use, kind of critical and strategic, and this would certainly be one of them. The footprint on the facility is larger than our current Cambridge facility, which is continuing to operate and will continue to produce by roughly 40%. It has additional acreage next to it and expansion capability as well. These two facilities in Ontario, we have an additional leased facility where we are executing work, and then an additional facility that we have in the United States. So, fabrication capacity is what we view as a differentiator for Aecon's nuclear capability. Candidly, if we are going to meet the needs of what is required here, some of the work absolutely needs to be taken off-site just to manage peaking levels. So, that is four facilities on the nuclear side of the house, and then we have an additional two facilities on the industrial side, one in Alberta and then one in Texas, where we are also looking to expand. So, this is all part of a long-term plan. Your first question was just around execution capacity. We are thinking about it from a technology standpoint, we are thinking about it from a system standpoint, we are thinking about it from a real asset standpoint, and as Jean-Louis mentioned, most importantly, we are thinking about it as people standpoint.
Jean-Louis Servranckx: Maybe I can add something on nuclear to close this question. Yes, the new build is important, but the real strong market for the years to come is what we call EPU, Extended Power Uprate, or life extension of the reactor. This is the best return for the utilities, is to invest in their existing reactor. Just consider that for each reactor, it represents something like CAD 1 billion, or less. We are present, of course, through this major component refurbishment program in Ontario, but we are now deeper and deeper in United States on this submarket, which is extremely important. We have more than 1,500 workers in the nuclear industry in U.S. at the moment, and it is quite important to highlight this point.
Chris Murray: Okay. That is very helpful. Thank you.
Operator: Thank you. One moment for the next question. Our next question is coming from the line of Michael Tupholme of TD Cowen. Please go ahead.
Michael Tupholme: Thank you. Good morning.
Jerome Julier: Hi.
Michael Tupholme: The first question is just around the outlook. You continue to call for further revenue growth in 2027. Just given that we're nearing the end of the year here, and given the strength of the backlog that you ended the third quarter with and the visibility that that gives you, is there any way to provide a little bit more detail around your expectations for top-line growth in 2027, how you see those evolving?
Jerome Julier: I'll talk about one. Aecon doesn't provide guidance, but maybe I'll give you some of the underlying factors that can at least help you give a pretty reasonable assumption. Out of the CAD 14.6 billion of backlog, our expectation is roughly CAD 5 billion will be executed in the next 12 months. In addition, we have something in the order of CAD 1.1 billion of recurring revenue programs, and that's obviously in the LTM, has been growing. Expect that to continue to grow. Those two together gives you a number, near CAD 6.1 billion. Aecon has a pretty strong history of, one, growing the work programs on the recurring revenue side, and then additionally securing additional work, and then additional change orders, and additional scopes on work that we have in progress as well. Historically, there's a broad range on these items, right? But if you kind of try to take somewhere like the P25 to P75, something in the CAD 750 million-CAD 1.2 billion range, that gives you an idea that there's something that could probably crest the CAD 7 billion mark.
Michael Tupholme: That's very helpful. Thank you. Just regarding the outlook, I guess, as it relates to new awards. Obviously, very strong backlog, record level. You talked in the prepared remarks about all of the various projects that are in the development phase, which give you some further visibility as those will eventually convert. Can you just speak about the demand environment today, as far as the conversations you're having for that next group of projects that could go into the development phase, or future awards? I understand the backlog's strong, what you've already been awarded that you're working toward getting to execution, but sort of that next group of projects that's going to kind of feed future years. What are you seeing there as far as activity levels, discussions, pipeline, et cetera?
Jean-Louis Servranckx: I will begin. Canada, globally, has decided to invest, and we have a Prime Minister who has just decided that it is his focus for the years to come. I would tend to say we are optimistic on our capacity to translate those development phases into execution of real projects. We have extremely strong team dedicated to those development phases, so we think that the rate of translating it is probably going to be quite high. I think it was the first part of your question. The second one was about equity?
Michael Tupholme: Sorry. Sorry, go ahead.
Jerome Julier: No, Mike, you just clarify the second part.
Michael Tupholme: Yeah. The second part was just, it is really a question around the demand environment as it relates to the conversations you are having now that are going to feed into that next round of awards, whether those are awards that get going right away or other projects that enter a development phase for a period of time. I am just trying to compare and contrast what you are seeing now versus maybe what you would have seen 12, 18 months ago. Again, I appreciate what you have secured and what you have in the development pipeline is already very robust, and looking at other things that have yet to be awarded to you and how robust that looks.
Jean-Louis Servranckx: I think that covered the answer. Probably in my life, I have not seen such a dynamic situation for infrastructure construction in the five years to come.
Michael Tupholme: Okay. That is helpful. I will leave it there. Thank you.
Jean-Louis Servranckx: Thanks.
Operator: One moment, please, for the next question. Our next question is coming from the line of Sabahat Khan of RBC Capital Markets. Please go ahead.
Sabahat Khan: Thanks, and good morning. I guess on the line of questioning around the backlog and the outlook in Canada that management has been commenting on, I guess, when you look at the pipeline opportunities, we have all seen the headlines, are you comfortable with this level of backlog, and do you look at it as a relatively stable range even before some of those nation-building projects start to get into the mix here? Just trying to think about the ability to sustain it at these levels, and I think an optimistic way to look at it is, it is at a reasonable level even before we get into the procurement for some of the larger stuff that could come over the next several years. Just curious on how you're thinking about the pipeline of opportunities, and is it fair to assume much of the stuff we've been seeing in the headlines hasn't really even begun to make its way into the system yet? Thanks.
Jerome Julier: Yeah. I think you're thinking about it the right way, Sabahat. Current backlog, clearly it was just an exceptional quarter of conversion with regards to backlog additions. We tend to take kind of the 1,000-yard view on this one, which is backlog on any given period is going to be lumpy. An expectation of kind of like a continuously high kind of book-to-bill ratio, exceeding like 3x. If we look LTM to LTM, 2024 to 2025 or 2025 to 2026, we were at kind of 2x or 1.6x. These are really astronomical levels. We're not really focused on the actual backlog number per se. I think it's like something that others are quite focused on. It's a helpful indicator of work to come. I think we can say with a high degree of certainty, Aecon's got a comfortable level of work to execute in front of it. On that basis, it's not kind of like a daily thing to be tracked. That being said, could it flex up or down by amounts in any given quarter? Yes. I don't think people should be focused on it. Given what we have in front of us with regards to projects and validation or development, we could see pretty chunky additions that could press the number upwards. That being said, as you can see by the overall productivity of Aecon, we're also a business that can basically deliver a lot of revenue, which drives it down. I think on a quarter-to-quarter basis, it's really hard to tell where that's going to land. I'd say just don't focus on it too much, but it's definitely a possibility to continue to move up.
Sabahat Khan: Thanks. Just for my follow-up, just looking at the recurring revenue just above the CAD 1 billion range. Now, can you talk about, is this a number that, given the, I guess, framework agreement, master service agreement nature of this work, this is something we can think about over the medium term? How do the adds to this line item work? Just trying to think of the growth algo over the next few years. Should we just assume like recurring revenue back up to over CAD 1 billion? Probably a fair amount to think about when we look ahead 2027 and 2028. Thanks.
Jean-Louis Servranckx: I think you are right, and I think we spoke about it, when we started. This CAD 1 billion, mainly is coming from utilities, mainly those MSAs are three years duration, and mainly speaking, the rate of renewal is extremely high. It is nearer to 90%-95%. Yes, it comes back naturally to the top-line. Coming back to utilities, when you just realize the growth in terms of revenue, but also the quality and the predictability of the margin to come in utilities, you probably understand why in Q2 2026, we decided to buy back Oaktree share. We negotiated it in Q2, and we are going to execute it in Q4. We had perfectly understood the trend that was coming.
Sabahat Khan: Thanks so much.
Jerome Julier: [Thanks Sabahat]
Operator: Thank you. Our next question will be coming from the line of Frederic Bastien of Raymond James. Please go ahead.
Jerome Julier: Hello, Mr. Bastien.
Frederic Bastien: Oh, thank you. Good morning. Guys, your plans to expand fabrication capacity in Ontario builds on a purchase of a facility in South Carolina earlier this summer. Can you put some numbers around these investments? Specifically, what was your fabrication capacity entering the year? How much are you hoping to add with these two investments?
